claims.text: Phase-selective recrystallization can overcome limited ductility in a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
A short, carefully controlled annealing treatment can selectively recrystallize the ductile phase.
Selective recrystallization reduces dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces.
Reducing interfacial dislocation pile-ups decreases local stress concentrations and suppresses microcrack nucleation.
The treatment can maintain or increase strength while improving ductility.
The starting alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, such as FCC/B2.
Dislocation accumulation at internal boundaries causes room-temperature brittleness in the starting alloy.
An optimized intermediate annealing temperature and dwell time can recrystallize the softer phase without coarsening or degrading the hard phase.
The proposed effect applies under quasi-static room-temperature tensile loading.
Phase-selective recrystallization forms a fully recrystallized soft phase within a hard-phase skeleton.
The recrystallized soft phase is refined.
Selective recrystallization creates cleaner and more coherent lamellar interfaces.
Recrystallization resets the defect structure of the soft phase and removes pre-existing pile-ups.
Phase-selective recrystallization releases the strain-hardening capacity of the duplex phases by eliminating weak boundaries.
Alleviating phase-boundary stress concentrations allows the alloy to sustain larger tensile strains.
The treated alloy will have markedly greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will maintain or slightly increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Excessive annealing can coarsen the microstructure or destroy the lamellar architecture and negate the benefits.
